newsitem.title: INDONESIA: SE Asian Grain - Domestic prices trend steady.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - Domestic prices trend steady.

text.p: Regional grains and oilseeds prices were holding steady in a quiet market as buyers kept a wary eye on falling futures prices in the United States, traders said on Wednesday.

Indonesian corn prices were steady as the harvest in East Java drew to a close, traders said. Corn was quoted around 420-425 rupiah/kg in Jakarta, compared with 415-420 rupiah a week ago. Soymeal was stable at around 850 rupiah/kg.
"There's been not much business in corn as buyers are generally taking a wait-and-see position due to the prevailing bearish tone in international markets," one Indonesian trader said.
"Buyers are waiting for prices to touch bottom, and might want to buy gingerly in amounts of 2,000 to 3,000 tonnes," the trader said. "There won't be any significant buying."
Local buyers also seemed well-covered until the end of the year. According to data from Tanjung Priok port in Jakarta, 5,370 tonnes of Argentine-origin soymeal arrived at the port on October 10.

In Malaysia, dealers in Kuala Lumpur could not report any purchases over the last week with their sights fixed on the sharp drop in prices in Chicago. Local prices remained little changed since the start of October.
"A" grade wheat in bags was trading at 840 ringgit per tonne ex-factory/godown central region. Low-grade wheat was quoted at 500-510 ringgit a tonne.
Local soymeal was at 818 ringgit a tonne. Imported soymeal was going for about 810 ringgit.
Bulk corn was trading at 500-505 ringgit.
One dealer said he expected December corn futures in the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) to drop to $2.60 per bushel and the December wheat contract to $3.90 a bushel by next week.
The December CBOT corn contract closed on Tuesday 1/2 U.S. cent higher at $2.79-1/2 a bushel. The December CBOT wheat contract was down one cent at $3.99-1/2 a bushel.
In Thailand, however, soymeal prices slipped lower as more feed protein ingredients arrived. Corn prices also fell as some feed producers switched to cheaper sources, trade sources said.
Thai soymeal was quoted around 10.20-10.30 baht a kg from 10.40 baht last week, they said.
The ship Kapitan Anistratenko arrived at a Thai port on Tuesday with 9,557 tonnes of India-origin rapeseed meal, groundnut meal and sunflower meal, traders said.
But so far, there have been no new orders as the industry waited for the dust to settle on the government's new policy on imports of certain feed ingredients before making any moves.
The cabinet on October 15 removed the import quota on feed raw material and sliced import tariffs on soybean, soymeal and corn, effective from November 1.
But a senior Commerce Ministry official warned the schedule could be delayed due to the bureaucracy involved in issuing the decree.

"I hope the government will do everything to meet the announced date," said one feed producer. "We aren't making new orders now, not because we have enough supply to cover short-term needs, but because we'd rather wait to make sure that our new imports will be subjected to the new tariff."
One trader said the industry might also be sidelined waiting for soybean prices to dip further on bullish U.S. crop prospects before placing fresh orders.
Corn prices, in the meantime, dropped to 4.40-4.45 baht a kg this week compared to 4.70-4.75 baht a kg last week.
Industry sources said feed producers helped push corn prices down through slower purchases and by switching to cheaper substitutes such as rice bran.
